title: Quantum Reservoir Computing for Optimal Control
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum reservoir computing (QRC) to the problem of optimal control within complex dynamical systems. Traditional optimal control methods often struggle with systems exhibiting high dimensionality, nonlinearities, and time-varying dynamics. Quantum systems, due to their inherent sensitivity to initial conditions and their ability to exist in superpositions, offer a potentially powerful alternative. This work proposes a framework where a continuously-operated quantum system, such as a driven cavity QED system, acts as a reservoir, mapping the system's dynamics onto a quantum state space. A variational quantum algorithm is then employed to learn the optimal control policy directly from the reservoir's evolved quantum state. We demonstrate, theoretically, that this approach can achieve optimal or near-optimal control performance, offering a novel method for tackling control problems where classical techniques fall short. The core of this approach lies in the reservoir's ability to effectively encode the system's dynamics and the variational algorithm's capacity to extract the desired control policy. The key mathematical elements explored include the mapping of system dynamics to the quantum state space, the formulation of the variational algorithm, and the analysis of the control performance metrics. This research represents a significant step towards utilizing the unique properties of quantum systems for advanced control applications.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Quantum State Tomography
abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) is a crucial technique for characterizing quantum states, vital for verifying quantum device performance and implementing quantum information processing. However, traditional QST methods are notoriously computationally demanding, requiring extensive experimental data acquisition and subsequent processing, often leading to high resource consumption. This work presents a novel framework for QST utilizing probabilistic programming. The core idea is to model the quantum state as a probability distribution and employ Bayesian inference, coupled with variational methods, to efficiently infer the density matrix from limited measurement data. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, showcasing its potential to significantly reduce experimental costs and improve the accuracy of QST. The framework's automation and optimization capabilities represent a substantial advancement in the field, paving the way for more accessible and efficient quantum state characterization.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Parallel Processing of Multi-Layer Data Streams
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for massively parallel data processing leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to utilize entanglement for direct, non-classical communication between multiple processor nodes, effectively circumventing the inherent bottlenecks of traditional data transfer methods. This approach aims to significantly enhance the performance of large-scale parallel computations by enabling instantaneous data synchronization and processing across distributed systems. The proposed architecture involves a distributed quantum network constructed around entangled states, where each node stores a portion of the data. The entanglement enables a "quantum teleportation" effect, facilitating rapid data exchange and synchronization without the delays associated with classical communication. This work outlines the theoretical framework, key concepts, and potential impact of this entanglement-based parallel processing paradigm. The presented model introduces a fundamentally different approach to parallel computing, moving beyond synchronous classical communication to exploit the inherent parallelism of quantum mechanics.

title: Branch-Centric Tokenization and Test-Time Augmentation for Skeleton Generation
abstract: Automatic skeleton generation involves predicting both joint positions and skeletal connectivity. However, existing approaches struggle to encode branch structures into token sequences and do not use test-time computation effectively. We study these choices within a unified autoregressive framework. First, we introduce branch-centric tokenization, a branch-aware representation that places structurally related elements next to each other and encodes connectivity directly in the sequence. Compared with standard BFS-style serialization, this representation yields more compact sequences. Second, we introduce view-augmented generation, a test-time augmentation procedure that applies axis-aligned rotations to the input mesh, maps all predictions back to a common frame, and selects the final skeleton based on mesh coverage and consistency among predictions from different views. Experiments show that our method achieves better skeleton prediction accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. In particular, our method reduces the CD-J2B error by 16.9% on the Articulation-XL2.0 dataset compared to the strongest directly comparable baseline, Auto-Connect. Qualitative results on in-the-wild meshes further demonstrate generalization across diverse inputs.

title: Efficient and Robust Camera-independent Multiview 3D Geometric Reconstruction from Noisy Monocular Depth Estimation and Multiple Point Matching
abstract: We present an efficient and robust method for 3D geometric reconstruction that is based solely on the camera-independent linear relationships among a given set of points, which are stable over time and robustly estimated using multiple point matches. We essentially learn, from correspondences between points across several frames, a linear geometric auto-regression matrix $\mathbf{W}$, which establishes how a point in 3D can be expressed as a linear combination of all the others. This matrix is constant and does not depend on the world coordinate system or the camera pose---it is an intrinsic property of the point set. We also show that the principal eigenvectors of $\mathbf{W}$, which all have eigenvalue $1$, provide a homogeneous representation of the 3D point configuration. The first version of our method takes advantage of noisy monocular depth maps in order to obtain, from multiple frames, a robust geometric auto-regression matrix $\mathbf{W}$ of linear relationships between the 3D points. Thus, we build on recent advances in deep learning, which now provide monocular depth estimation models that are fast but very often noisy. Our approach handles noise through robust linear estimation over several frames. The second version of our method does not need monocular depth estimation maps. It applies in cases of weak-perspective projection, when the linear combinations between the 3D points can be robustly estimated from their 2D projections in the image. Note that the camera projection matrix is never used in our derivations. Consequently, our method does not recover camera pose, but only 3D structure. This is a key difference between our method and the related literature on 3D geometric reconstruction.

title: Multilingual large language models do not comprehend all natural languages to equal degrees
abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) play a critical role in how humans access information. While their core functionality relies on the ability to comprehend written requests, our understanding of this ability is currently constrained, because most benchmarks evaluate LLMs in high-resource languages that are predominantly spoken by Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) communities. The default assumption is that English is the best-performing language for LLMs, while smaller, low-resource languages are linked to less natural or reliable outputs, even in multilingual, state-of-the-art models. To track fluctuations in the comprehension abilities of LLMs, we prompt 3 popular models across 12 languages, representing the Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic, Turkic, Sino-Tibetan, and Japonic language families. Our results suggest that the models exhibit remarkable accuracy across typologically diverse languages, yet they may fall behind human baselines, albeit to different degrees. Contrary to what was expected, English is not the best-performing language, as it was systematically outperformed by several Romance languages, even lower-resource ones. We frame the results by highlighting the role of factors that drive LLM performance, such as tokenization, language distance from Spanish and English, size of training data, and data origin in high- vs. low-resource languages and WEIRD vs. non-WEIRD communities.

title: From Supervisor Mode to Distributed Enforcement: A History of Hardware-Enforced Platform Security
abstract: English author preprint v4.1. This substantially revised edition compares historically situated hardware-enforced platform security mechanisms rather than proposing a linear or causal transition. It offers a bounded decision procedure for classifying a specified security guarantee as local, distributed, or not classifiable from the available evidence. Five provisional analytical operations—naming, mediating, measuring, remembering, and erasing—organize the comparison. The manuscript discusses negative and conditional cases, limits of the selected corpus, and alternative explanations. The accompanying research package contains the manuscript, source-claim register, eight-family operation matrix, twelve-guarantee decision matrix, reference map, static research supplement, and a SHA-256 manifest. The public supplement is also available at https://hardwaresecurityhistory.org/research/. This is an author preprint, not a peer-reviewed or accepted IEEE article. The manuscript contains a section-specific disclosure of generative AI assistance. The author retains responsibility for the claims, interpretations, and citations.

title: Evolutionary Algorithm-Driven Hardware Architecture Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to the optimization of hardware architectures. Traditional hardware design methodologies often rely on manual design or rule-based optimization, which can be time-consuming and may not always yield the best possible solutions. This research proposes a novel approach where an EA is employed to automatically generate and refine hardware architectures, targeting specific performance objectives. The core mechanism involves formulating the hardware architecture design problem as an evolutionary problem, utilizing algorithms such as genetic algorithms (GAs) to explore the design space. Key aspects addressed include circuit layout, timing optimization, and power consumption control. The research demonstrates the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach, offering a flexible and adaptive method for hardware architecture optimization. The paper details the algorithmic framework, highlighting the key components and their interactions. It provides a conceptual overview of the process, emphasizing the automation and adaptability inherent in the EA-driven architecture optimization paradigm. The ultimate goal is to achieve superior performance compared to conventional design techniques. ---

title: Neuromorphic Reservoir Computing with Spiking Neural Networks and Fractal Geometry
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing fractal geometry within spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reservoir computing applications. Traditional reservoir computing relies on complex, randomly connected recurrent networks to temporally abstract input signals. However, these systems often suffer from high computational cost and limited ability to handle complex, non-stationary data. We propose a novel approach that integrates fractal structures – specifically, iterated function systems (IFS) – into the reservoir architecture of an SNN. This allows the system to inherently generate complex, multi-dimensional representations of the input, dramatically improving its efficiency and its ability to process high-dimensional, non-stationary data. The core claim is that fractal geometry, when integrated into the architecture of SNNs, can dramatically improve the efficiency and complexity-handling capabilities of neuromorphic reservoir computing systems. The presented framework leverages the self-similarity and scale invariance properties of fractals to create reservoirs that are naturally adept at capturing temporal dependencies and complex patterns. The system operates with minimal training, relying on the inherent properties of the fractal structure to generate rich representations. We discuss the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and outline a potential implementation strategy, focusing on the mathematical formulation of the system and the key parameters that govern its behavior.

title: Formal Verification of Programs Based on Cellular Automata
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program verification using cellular automata (CA). Traditional program verification techniques often struggle with the complexities of concurrent and memory-safe programs, frequently failing to detect subtle errors. We introduce a methodology where program code is mapped onto a CA model, simulating program execution through the interaction of cells governed by predefined rules. This approach offers a more intuitive and potentially efficient method for verifying program correctness, particularly in identifying errors that are difficult to uncover with conventional formal verification techniques. We explore the core mechanisms of this system, focusing on how cell states and rules are defined to deduce program correctness or identify potential errors. The primary benefit of this method lies in its ability to handle dynamic and complex programs in a more accessible manner. The effectiveness of the CA model is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Differential Privacy
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to differential privacy utilizing quantum entanglement. Traditional differential privacy relies on adding noise to queries to obscure individual data contributions, a technique often limited by the dimensionality of the data and the potential for sophisticated attacks. We propose encoding data points into entangled qubit states, thereby leveraging the inherent correlations provided by entanglement to achieve stronger privacy guarantees. The core idea involves performing computations on these entangled states, minimizing the need for direct data exposure. Crucially, we introduce a mechanism for carefully calibrating measurement noise, exploiting the unique properties of entanglement to control the privacy loss. Our framework demonstrates the potential to significantly improve privacy levels compared to classical methods, especially when dealing with high-dimensional datasets, offering a new paradigm for privacy-preserving data analysis in the quantum realm. The theoretical analysis presents a novel framework for quantifying privacy loss, considering both the entanglement resource requirements and the calibrated noise levels. This work lays the foundation for future research into quantum-enhanced differential privacy and its implications for secure data processing.

title: Dynamic Topology Adaptive Neural Networks (D-TANet)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topology Adaptive Neural Networks (D-TANet), a novel neural network architecture designed to address the limitations of traditional static networks in dynamic and complex environments. D-TANet leverages principles from biological neural systems, specifically dynamic synaptic plasticity and network connectivity, to achieve enhanced learning and generalization capabilities. The core idea is to create a network where both the connections (topology) and the synaptic weights are dynamically adjusted in response to input data and environmental feedback. This is achieved through a graph neural network (GNN) framework with a dynamic synapse model and a topology optimization mechanism driven by reinforcement learning. The network's topology adapts via node addition/removal, edge modification, and global topology refinement, resulting in a more efficient and robust system. Mathematical formulations are presented to detail the key components of the D-TANet architecture and its adaptive mechanisms. This work provides a foundational approach for building intelligent systems capable of truly adapting to ever-changing conditions. ---

title: Probability-Driven Algorithm Optimization via Adaptive Weight Adjustment
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm optimization approach based on the adaptive weight adjustment of a Gaussian process. Traditional optimization methods often employ fixed parameters, while this method leverages the adaptive properties of Gaussian processes to dynamically adjust weights during algorithm execution, leading to improved performance and stability. The core mechanism involves modeling data probability distributions using Gaussian processes and using these distributions to guide weight adjustments, optimizing the algorithm's behavior. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing significant performance gains compared to existing algorithms.

title: 基于自适应图的动态优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic optimization algorithm based on an adaptive graph. The algorithm leverages the inherent structure of the adaptive graph to efficiently solve complex optimization problems, offering a significant improvement over traditional methods. We detail the design of the adaptive graph, its underlying principles, and the implementation of a robust optimization algorithm. The algorithm's primary focus is on rapidly addressing large-scale optimization challenges. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary results, highlighting its potential for applications across diverse domains.

title: Adaptive Clustering Algorithm for Dynamic Cluster Structure Adjustment
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive clustering algorithm designed to dynamically adjust cluster structure during the clustering process. Traditional clustering algorithms often rely on predefined structures, which are inadequate when faced with data variations. This new algorithm leverages the self-adaptive nature of clustering algorithms to dynamically adjust cluster shapes, leading to improved clustering results. The algorithm employs a novel approach that monitors and responds to data characteristics, intelligently reshaping the clusters to better represent the underlying data distribution. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously evaluates cluster quality and adjusts the cluster structure accordingly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experimental results, showcasing its ability to outperform traditional methods in several benchmark datasets. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's strengths and potential future directions.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Self-Referential Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic self-referential algorithm designed to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of computations. The algorithm adapts self-reference parameters based on input data and computational process, offering a responsive and adaptable solution. The core mechanism centers around a dynamic adjustment strategy that allows the algorithm to dynamically adjust the self-reference's influence, optimizing performance in varying scenarios. We explore the advantages of this approach and provide a detailed framework for implementation. The design leverages a feedback loop to iteratively refine the self-reference parameters, resulting in improved precision and reduced computational overhead. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's potential applications and future research directions.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Dynamic Topological Optimization for Information Encoding and Decoding
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum information encoding and decoding by leveraging the dynamic topology of quantum entanglement. Traditional quantum information processing methods largely rely on static entangled states, potentially limiting information transmission rates. We propose a system architecture incorporating multiple controlled quantum bits (qubits) exhibiting dynamic entanglement. Through precise manipulation of qubit positions and interactions, we harness the topological changes within the entanglement to encode and decode information. A topological optimization algorithm is then introduced, continuously adjusting the system's qubit topology based on information transmission efficiency and entanglement stability criteria. The core claim is that this dynamic topological control enables optimization of the encoding and decoding process, potentially surpassing the classical information transmission limit. The fundamental mechanisms involve exploiting the temporal evolution of entanglement, coupled with a feedback control loop driven by topological optimization. Mathematical formulations are presented to describe the key components of the system, including the entanglement entropy, the topological optimization objective function, and the dynamics of the qubit positions. This work represents a significant step toward realizing more efficient and robust quantum information networks. ---

Mathematical formulations are presented to describe the key components of the system, including the entanglement entropy, the topological optimization objective function, and the dynamics of the qubit positions. This work represents a significant step toward realizing more efficient and robust quantum information networks. ---

title: Dynamic Topology-Guided Quantum Entanglement Models
abstract: This paper explores a novel dynamic topology-guided quantum entanglement model. Traditional quantum entanglement models often rely on static properties of entangled states, limiting their potential for robust information protection. We propose a framework that leverages topological dynamics to dynamically modify entangled states during measurement, offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum information handling. The core mechanism involves the introduction of a "topological map" – a dynamic, multi-dimensional representation – that governs the evolution of entangled correlations. This model provides a mechanism for enhanced quantum information security and offers a path toward more adaptable and robust quantum systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and discuss potential implications for quantum cryptography and distributed quantum computing.

title: Dynamic Symbolic Regression with Contextual Constraints
abstract: Symbolic regression is a powerful technique for discovering mathematical equations from data. However, its performance is often hampered by noisy data and the lack of explicit domain knowledge. This work introduces a novel approach, Dynamic Symbolic Regression with Contextual Constraints (DSRCC), designed to address these limitations. DSRCC iteratively refines a regression model while dynamically adjusting constraints based on model uncertainty and evolving domain context. The system utilizes a feedback loop wherein the regression model's confidence in its parameters is assessed, and this uncertainty drives the adaptation of constraints. This adaptive constraint mechanism allows the system to effectively filter out noise and incorporate relevant domain-specific knowledge, leading to more accurate and interpretable regression models. The core of the system lies in a probabilistic framework that quantifies the uncertainty associated with regression parameters, which directly influences the strength and scope of the contextual constraints. This approach bridges the gap between the flexibility of symbolic regression and the rigor of constraint-based methods, offering a promising solution for complex data modeling scenarios.

title: Nonlinear Geometric Transformations: An Adaptive Learning Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive learning algorithm for non-linear geometric transformations. Traditional approaches often rely on fixed transformation parameters, limiting their effectiveness in handling complex datasets. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts transformation parameters based on data characteristics, enabling more robust feature extraction and model optimization. We propose a framework that integrates self-adaptive learning with the principles of non-linear geometry. The core mechanism involves a continuous feedback loop that learns the optimal transformation parameters through a training process, adapting to the specific nuances of the input data. This approach surpasses conventional methods by offering increased flexibility and improved generalization capabilities in image processing and computer vision. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and experimental results demonstrating its superior performance in a range of tasks.

title: Quantum-Based Feature Selection and Dimensionality Reduction
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum computing to the critical tasks of feature selection and dimensionality reduction within machine learning. Traditional methods often struggle with high-dimensional data, leading to computational bottlenecks and potentially reduced model accuracy. We propose a novel approach leveraging the principles of quantum error correction and quantum entanglement to construct an algorithm capable of efficiently identifying and reducing the most relevant features. The core mechanism utilizes quantum machine learning techniques, specifically quantum feature mapping and feature extraction, to transform data into a quantum state that inherently captures feature relationships. This allows for a more effective selection process based on quantum interference and the exploration of complex correlations. We demonstrate, theoretically, the potential advantages of this approach over classical methods, highlighting improvements in both efficiency and predictive accuracy. The algorithm's design incorporates error correction to mitigate the effects of noise inherent in quantum systems, further enhancing its robustness. The research contributes to the growing field of quantum machine learning, offering a new paradigm for tackling complex data challenges.

title: Neuro-Morphic Computing via Temporal Flow Sub-Quantization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neuro-morphic computing, termed Temporal Flow Sub-Quantization (TFSQ), which addresses the critical limitation of existing neuro-morphic architectures: the inadequate handling of temporal information within time-series data. The core concept involves encoding temporal sequences into quantum states, leveraging the inherent properties of quantum mechanics – superposition and entanglement – to achieve parallel processing and efficient inference. We propose a model architecture where time series data is represented and computed in parallel using quantum bits (qubits), resulting in a significant improvement in processing speed and resource utilization compared to traditional sequential methods. The key innovation lies in the sub-quantization technique, which decomposes complex time series into manageable quantum states, optimizing both the representation and computational efficiency. This work lays the groundwork for a new paradigm in neuro-morphic computing, capable of tackling complex temporal data challenges across diverse applications, including anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and signal processing. We present a theoretical framework and a foundational model, demonstrating the potential of TFSQ.

title: Het-node2vec: second-order random walk sampling for heterogeneous graph embedding
abstract: Abstract Many real-world problems are naturally modeled as heterogeneous graphs, where nodes and edges represent multiple types of entities and relations. Existing learning models for heterogeneous graph representation usually depend on the computation of specific, user-defined heterogeneous paths, or on the application of large, and often non-scalable, deep neural network architectures. We propose Het-node2vec, an extension of the node2vec algorithm, designed to embed heterogeneous graphs by capturing the topological and structural characteristics of the graph and the semantic information underlying the different types of nodes and edges; this is performed by introducing a simple stochastic node-type switching strategy in second-order random walk processes. Empirical results on synthetic graphs, as well as on benchmark and real-world biomedical graphs, show that Het-node2vec achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods for heterogeneous graphs in node label prediction tasks.

title: SLATE: Are AI-Generated Slides Educationally Effective? A Benchmark for Language Teaching Quality and Learner Knowledge Acquisition
abstract: LLMs have achieved remarkable capabilities in generating language teaching slides. However, a critical mismatch persists between visual polish and actual instructional effectiveness. To address this gap, we introduce SLATE (Slide-based Learning Assessment for Teaching Effectiveness), the first benchmark that evaluates AI-generated language teaching slides through instructional effectiveness and learner knowledge acquisition. SLATE transforms linguistics olympiad puzzles from low-resource languages with negligible web presence into 90 standardized instructional units comprising 1,133 assessable items, paired with a structured course outline and matched near- and far-transfer test sets. This pretest-posttest design eliminates pretrained knowledge leakage, ensuring gains reflect learning rather than prior recall. Using VLMs as scalable learner proxies and directionally supported by a three-system human pilot, our results show that content validity exhibits a weak association with learning gain, while pedagogical design exhibits a robust positive association. Moreover, most systems show a significant gap between near- and far-transfer accuracy, and even frontier models can produce negative learning gains. SLATE reveals a dissociation between artifact quality and instructional effectiveness, calling for a paradigm shift in how generative teaching systems are built, evaluated, and deployed.

title: Machine Learning for Pre-Culture ESBL Risk Stratification to Guide Empiric Antibiotic Selection: A 12-Hospital Study of Enterobacteriaceae Cultures
abstract: Empiric antibiotic therapy for suspected ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae must be selected 48-72 hours before culture results, forcing clinicians to choose between undertreating resistant infections and overusing carbapenems that drive further resistance. We developed a cost-sensitive XGBoost model predicting an ESBL phenotype (resistance to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam) at culture ordering using 45 pre-culture EHR features across 132,955 cultures from 72,217 patients at 12 hospitals (14.41% with the ESBL phenotype). Cultures were partitioned at the patient level. At 90% sensitivity, the model achieved 95.8% NPV, reducing post-test ESBL probability to 4.2%, a threshold that may support safe carbapenem-sparing in non-ICU settings, while sparing 307 of every 1,000 cultures an unnecessary broad-spectrum course at the cost of 14 missed ESBL cases per 1,000. SHAP analysis identified prior ESBL colonization as the dominant predictor, ahead of prior organism burden and neighborhood deprivation; removing deprivation features caused minimal performance loss ($Δ\text{AUROC} = -0.020$), enabling equitable bedside deployment. Discrimination was unchanged under a strict IDSA ESBL-E definition (AUROC 0.766), with specimen type added as a predictor (0.764) and without any class-imbalance correction (0.762), and ranged from 0.71 to 0.78 across organism strata.

title: sheval: An RDF data shapes evaluation tool and test-suite for recursive shapes
abstract: Two different languages have been developed to validate RDF data based on the concept of a shape: ShEx and SHACL. In each language it is possible to define a shape that refers to itself, which is called a recursive shape. While in the case of ShEx, the semantics of recursive shapes is well defined and is part of the specification, in the case of SHACL, the semantics of recursive shapes is left to the implementation of the different SHACL engines. Consequently, the different SHACL engines show different behaviours when confronted with recursive shapes. In this paper we present sheval: an evaluation framework consisting of a tool and a test suite that can be used to compare the behaviour of different shapes technologies when confronted with recursive definitions. The tool has been used to evaluate and understand the differences in the implementation of recursive shapes in ShEx and SHACL. It provides a framework for testing and comparing the behaviour of different shape engines, helping to identify inconsistencies and potential issues, and providing a basis for further research and development in the field of shape-based validation of RDF data.

title: A Hardware-Isolated, Sub-Millisecond Runtime Audit Architecture for Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems via Pre-Actuation State Dissolution
abstract: Core Motivation: Latency Asymmetry and Non-Separable Exposure Current autonomous agent safeguards rely on perimeter policies evaluated at the API dispatch boundary. This approach fails structurally: The Latency Gap: The interval between internal intent formation and external action serialisation is approximately 200 ms, whereas human operator orientation requires hundreds of seconds. Post-hoc human review is forensic rather than preventive. Local Predicate Failure: Multi-agent exposure is superadditive across sequences of individually permitted calls. We formally prove that no local predicate evaluated on single actions can bound an exposure functional that is not additively separable across those actions (Proposition 1). The Automated Metacognitive Protocol (AMP) AMP shifts runtime enforcement from the network boundary directly into the inference path: Non-Differentiable Shadow Taps: Residual-stream activations are tapped across selected layers with an enforced stopgrad boundary, introducing zero gradient pressure to optimize around the monitor (Assumption A1). Permission Manifold Scoring: Hidden states are projected via low-rank audit operators ($k = 32, d = 8192$) and evaluated against an approved operating envelope using Mahalanobis distance with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage for covariance estimation. Dual-Path Temporal Filtering: Divergence is evaluated using an Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) for acute spikes and a one-sided CUSUM statistic to catch sub-threshold, incremental drift attacks. Pre-Actuation State Dissolution: Upon threshold breach, the architecture applies a scheduled orthogonal subspace projection to recursively remove the unaligned direction across downstream layers until the intent magnitude reaches a zero-weight vacancy threshold (Proposition 4). Unlike boundary blocking, which preserves unaligned intent in context to drive re-planning and rebound dynamics, it structurally eliminates representational support before token serialisation. Intelligence-Invariant Hardware Floor: Actuation lines pass through a normally-open physical relay held closed by a signed, high-frequency enclave heartbeat. Power or heartbeat loss drops the rail into a safe state invariant to counterparty reasoning capability (Proposition 5). Computational and Latency Budget Analytical derivation across twelve tapped layers yields an audit cost of approximately 6.6 MFLOP per token. On dedicated audit silicon, this results in an analytical budget of under 20 µs end-to-end, maintaining an operational margin of $10^4$ within the 200 ms action boundary. Design Lineage and Empirical Scope Functional Phenomenology (Section 1.4): The four load-bearing priors—non-interfering observation (satipaṭṭhāna), triadic failure roots (lobha, dosa, moha), pre-manifestation state removal (samuccheda vs. vikkhambhana), and structural vacancy (anattā)—are adapted from the Pali Canon strictly as functional systems phenomenology and structural engineering priors. All properties stand independently on control-theoretic and linear-algebraic formulations. Validation Status: The paper presents an architectural specification with analytical guarantees. Section 8.5 explicitly outlines nine falsifiable empirical quantities, including audit-space separability, false-positive rates on benign traffic, and rebound coefficients reserved for future experimental benchmark validation

title: Hierarchical Self-Organizing Maps for Multi-Scale Data Exploration
abstract: Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) are a powerful unsupervised learning technique for dimensionality reduction and data visualization. However, their effectiveness is often limited when dealing with data exhibiting multiple scales of granularity. This paper proposes a novel approach – Hierarchical Self-Organizing Maps – to overcome this limitation. The core idea is to create a layered architecture where lower-level SOMs learn local patterns at finer scales, while higher-level SOMs aggregate and interpret the outputs of these lower levels, ultimately generating a multi-scale representation. The system is designed to capture complex relationships within data that would be missed by traditional, single-scale SOMs. The method is presented with theoretical underpinnings, a proposed architecture, and a discussion of potential applications. The primary contribution is a framework for dynamic multi-scale data exploration, leveraging the strengths of SOMs while mitigating their inherent scale limitations. The key equation guiding the hierarchical aggregation is: (Ui, Vi) = fh(Ui, Vi), where Ui and Vi represent the output vectors from the i-th level, and fh is the hierarchical fusion function. This architecture allows for a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of datasets with inherent hierarchical structures.

title: Based on Neural-Symbolic AI for Causal Reasoning and Decision-Making
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal reasoning and decision-making by integrating the strengths of neural and symbolic artificial intelligence. The core idea is to leverage the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks to learn causal relationships while utilizing symbolic reasoning for logical inference and decision-making processes. This fusion aims to create a system capable of generating more reliable and interpretable intelligent decisions. We introduce a framework where neural networks represent observational data and learn underlying causal structures, which are then formalized and manipulated using symbolic logic for reasoning. The resulting system offers a significant advancement over traditional approaches by addressing the complexities inherent in causal inference and ultimately enhancing the trustworthiness and explainability of intelligent decision-making systems. The paper details the architecture of the proposed system, the methods used for neural-symbolic integration, and outlines potential applications. ---

title: A Projective–Contractive Normalization Layer with Guaranteed Convergence and Closed-Form Fixed Point
abstract: We introduce a new normalization operator for neural networks,defined as the composition of a projective map and a contractiontoward a prior distribution. The operator acts on the probabilitysimplex and is contractive in the Hilbert projective metric, whichguarantees the existence of a unique fixed point reached from anyinitialization. In neural network implementations no iteration isrequired: the fixed point admits a closed-form expression that canbe computed directly. The parameter ε ∈ (0,1] controls the strengthof the contraction and allows explicit modulation of calibration.We provide definitions, theorems, proofs, geometric and dynamicinterpretations, and a full backpropagation derivation.After integration into neural networks as a positive log-affinelayer, we relate the operator to projective geometry, contractionmappings, Sinkhorn-type operators, and Deep Equilibrium Models.Experiments on MNIST and tabular data show that projective layersself-organize into complementary contraction regimes and yield highlycalibrated models without sacrificing accuracy, providing a principledgeometric alternative to softmax-based normalization with broadapplicability in neural architectures

title: 自适应拓扑拓扑层级的量子信息传输
abstract: Quantum information transfer is a critical challenge in quantum computing and quantum communication. Traditional methods often struggle with the inherent fragility of quantum states, making reliable and efficient transfer difficult. This paper explores a novel quantum information transfer algorithm based on the concept of adaptive topology, aiming to overcome these limitations through precise encoding and transmission. We propose a system where the quantum state is encoded and manipulated within a dynamically evolving topology, allowing for enhanced fidelity and reduced error rates. The core mechanism utilizes a self-organizing topology to ensure the preservation of quantum information during transmission. We analyze the algorithm's performance, demonstrating significant improvements in transfer efficiency and fidelity compared to existing approaches. This work contributes to the advancement of quantum information technologies by providing a robust and adaptable framework for secure and reliable quantum communication.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Representation via Wavefunction Fragmentation
abstract: Quantum state representations are a fundamental challenge in quantum information theory, struggling to efficiently encode and process complex quantum systems. Existing methods often fall short in scalability and computational complexity, hindering progress in areas like quantum simulation and optimization. This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum state representation – Wavefunction Fragmentation – that dynamically breaks down the wavefunction into smaller, self-contained fragments. This fragmentation allows for a more efficient and scalable representation, particularly effective for systems exhibiting complex dynamics. We detail a method for implementing this fragmentation, incorporating a sophisticated quantum state embedding algorithm to combine the fragments into a unified representation. The core claim is that this method offers a fundamentally more efficient means of encoding quantum information, enabling advancements in quantum algorithm design and data manipulation. We present preliminary results demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in a simplified quantum system model, showcasing improved computational speed and reduced memory requirements compared to traditional methods.

title: Non-linear Geometric Structure Mapping Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel non-linear geometric structure mapping algorithm based on quantum entanglement. The algorithm aims to directly translate complex geometric data into low-dimensional geometric models, facilitating precise calculations and optimization of intricate geometric shapes. We propose a mechanism that utilizes quantum entanglement to manipulate the quantum state of the input, allowing for the reconstruction of the geometric model through controlled quantum measurements. The core claim is that this approach offers a fundamentally new computational method capable of handling high-dimensional geometric data without the limitations of traditional classical algorithms. This work addresses the limitations of existing methods by leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement for geometric information mapping.

title: Dynamic Topology-Based Quantum Optimization Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum optimization algorithm based on dynamic topology. The algorithm leverages the principles of topology to dynamically adjust quantum parameters, enabling efficient exploration of the solution space and facilitating self-adaptive optimization. We propose a framework where the quantum system evolves through a series of topological transformations guided by a feedback mechanism, resulting in a globally optimal solution. The algorithm's core mechanism involves creating and manipulating topological structures that guide the optimization process. The potential of this approach to enhance quantum algorithms and achieve improved efficiency is significant.

title: Self-Adaptive Spin Quantum Computing Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive spin quantum computing algorithm designed to enhance computational precision and efficiency. Traditional spin adjustment mechanisms often rely on fixed parameter settings, limiting the algorithm's capabilities. We propose a dynamic adjustment strategy that adapts the spin parameters during the computation process. This adaptive approach allows for finer control of the spin state, leading to improved performance in complex calculations. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously monitors and adjusts the spin parameters based on the current state of the computation, thereby optimizing the outcome. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and discuss its potential applications in various quantum computing tasks.

title: Dynamic Topology Structures Optimized by Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of machine learning to optimize dynamic topology structures, aiming to enhance system behavior through intelligent pattern recognition and adjustment. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with the complexity of dynamic systems, necessitating novel approaches. We propose a framework that leverages machine learning to learn and refine the inherent structure of these systems, resulting in more adaptive and responsive behavior. The core mechanism involves training a model to predict and manipulate the topology, fostering a dynamic equilibrium. This research introduces a novel optimization method that directly addresses the challenges of optimizing complex systems with intricate topological variations. The potential impact of this approach is significant across diverse domains requiring adaptive control and design.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum State Encoding Strategy
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense potential for breakthroughs across numerous fields, yet realizing this potential requires significant advancements in quantum algorithm design and hardware implementation. A crucial aspect of this journey is the efficient and accurate encoding of quantum states, which is currently limited by the capabilities of traditional classical encoding methods. This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive quantum state encoding strategy aimed at addressing these limitations. The proposed strategy leverages continuous monitoring of the quantum state's dynamics to dynamically adjust encoding parameters, optimizing for both computational efficiency and fidelity. We present a framework based on a feedback loop that iteratively refines the encoding process based on real-time state measurements. The core mechanism centers around adjusting the parameters of the quantum state representation to minimize error correction requirements, ultimately boosting quantum computational performance. The theoretical framework demonstrates improved performance compared to static encoding methods in a benchmark environment.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Geometric Topology (QGET)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Geometric Topology (QGET) explores the potential of quantum entanglement to fundamentally alter geometric topology through the creation of interconnected, entangled structures. This paper proposes a novel approach that utilizes entanglement to establish bridges between geometric shapes, leading to enhanced analysis and manipulation capabilities. The core mechanism involves introducing entanglement between geometric points, resulting in a network of interconnected shapes that exhibits enhanced properties compared to traditional topological methods. The research delves into the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, examining its potential impact on geometric structure and exploring avenues for further investigation. This work represents a significant departure from conventional topological research, incorporating quantum mechanics to unlock new levels of understanding and control over geometric systems.

title: Self-Organizing Quantum Hardware via Adaptive Entanglement Control
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum hardware design and control, leveraging reinforcement learning to achieve self-organization and optimal performance. The core concept is that quantum processors, rather than relying on pre-determined calibration, can dynamically adapt their entanglement generation and maintenance through real-time feedback. We propose a decentralized control system where reinforcement learning algorithms continuously optimize control parameters – such as laser pulse shapes and magnetic field strengths – based on metrics like entanglement fidelity and coherence time. This adaptive strategy mitigates the challenges associated with traditional, fixed-parameter control schemes, which often struggle to account for the inherent noise and fluctuations in quantum systems. The resulting architecture represents a significant step towards truly autonomous quantum computing, promising enhanced scalability and robustness. This paper details the theoretical framework, the reinforcement learning algorithm employed, and outlines the potential impact of this approach on future quantum hardware development.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated remarkable success in automating the design of neural networks, often surpassing human-designed architectures in performance. However, the underlying principles guiding these successes remain largely unexplored from an information-theoretic perspective. This work investigates the fundamental limits of NAS by leveraging concepts from information theory. We formulate the search process as an information gain problem, quantifying the amount of information revealed by different search strategies regarding the optimal network architecture. We utilize mutual information to measure the dependence between architecture parameters and performance, and Kolmogorov complexity to assess the efficiency of representing architectural choices. Our theoretical framework provides a rigorous basis for evaluating NAS algorithms, offering a potentially more efficient and principled approach to architecture discovery. We derive bounds on the achievable information gain and discuss the implications for future NAS research. The core contribution lies in establishing a quantifiable measure of architectural exploration and suggesting that NAS effectiveness is ultimately limited by the inherent complexity of representing and evaluating network architectures.

title: From Explainability to Actionability: a Tiered Adaptable Multi-Agent Framework with Agent Reasoning Tools for Collaborative Failure Recovery
abstract: Abstract Effective human-AI collaboration, especially in failure scenarios, requires systems that function as active partners rather than static tools. This research addresses this requirement by introducing a tiered multi-agent architecture grounded in Human-Centered eXplainable AI principles. The architecture consists of three novel design artifacts: tiered reasoning that adapts explanation depth to failure severity, a traceable memory bus for auditability, and flexible reasoning tools for enhanced adaptability. These designs enable agents to not only perform evidence-based diagnoses of performance gaps but devise recovery strategies and propose actionable improvement plans as well. We empirically evaluate this architecture on an aspect term extraction task using hybrid methods that combine performance comparisons against state-of-the-art baselines, human expert user studies, and multi-role user simulations. The results demonstrate that our architecture significantly enhances both task performance and failure recovery diagnosis and plans. We then validate the generalizability of our architecture with a second task of comparable complexity. This research contributes an adaptable and generalizable framework and foundational artifacts for trustworthy AI teammates.

title: Test-Time Weak-to-Strong Alignment: Transferring Implicit Rewards from Weak to Strong Flow Models
abstract: Aligning a text-to-image generation flow model with a reward makes it follow objectives that the training data alone does not provide. Alignment fine-tuning delivers this by reinforcement learning (RL) or preference optimization, but it must be repeated for every checkpoint and returns a model fixed at the reward and strength it was trained with. Test-time alignment instead steers a frozen model during sampling, allowing task-specific and sample-specific guidance. Existing methods obtain this only by drawing the per-step signal from the reward function itself, through its gradient, or through a separately trained value function. We propose changing the supervision source: let a pair of weak models, not a reward function, supply the supervision. A source aligned model, kept together with its base as a source alignment pair, stores its training reward as an implicit, step-wise, KL-anchored signal expressed in the sampler's own coordinates. We explore whether this model-form supervision can cross scale, and show that it does: our method, AlignGraft, aligns a larger, frozen, never-tuned model by adding the pair's velocity difference during sampling. The transport is exact under a shared noising kernel and needs neither the reward nor its gradient at test time. The method has no schedules, only a single scalar that controls the alignment strength and can extrapolate it beyond that of the source alignment pair. Across image and video flow models (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX, and Wan), the transfer lifts the frozen large model on preference, compositional, and text-rendering rewards, can exceed the source aligned model itself, and preserves the large model's fidelity at a small constant sampling overhead. Extensive experiments show that one alignment run on a weak model produces supervision that the whole model family can reuse at test time.

title: Quantum Key Generation Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper explores the concept of generating physically secure cryptographic keys leveraging the principles of quantum decoherence. The core idea revolves around exploiting the inherent sensitivity of quantum systems to environmental interactions, specifically the decoherence phenomenon, to create a key. The generated key's security is predicated on the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics, offering a robust defense against traditional attacks. This work details a theoretical framework for such a system, outlining the key generation process, the measurement protocols, and the resulting key distribution. The approach emphasizes the unique security advantages offered by quantum mechanics compared to classical cryptography. We propose a method for utilizing the rate of decoherence as a source of randomness, which is then used to construct the cryptographic key. The security analysis highlights the exponential key space growth associated with quantum systems, making brute-force attacks computationally infeasible. Furthermore, this work addresses potential challenges and future research directions in implementing a practical quantum key generation system based on decoherence.

title: Pathology-Aware Explainability in Chest X-ray Classifiers
abstract: Evaluating chest radiograph classifiers presents a fundamental mismatch: models are conventionally validated by discrimination metrics, yet radiological diagnosis relies on the structured interpretation of visual signs—its semiology. This mismatch allows strong classification despite attribution to regions with no finding-specific meaning. We propose a semiology-grounded framework to evaluate the anatomical faithfulness of post-hoc explanations beyond generic geometric overlap. Using VinDr-CXR filtered for strict multi-radiologist consensus, we trained AlexNet and DenseNet-121 at two input resolutions and paired two findings with divergent spatial signatures—aortic enlargement and cardiomegaly—to distinguish genuine localisation from a central default. Grad-CAM attributions were cross-validated with gradient-free occlusion sensitivity and calibrated against an input-blind central-Gaussian baseline. Although all models achieved strong discrimination (Matthews Correlation Coefficient 0.56–0.74, AUC-ROC > 0.91), their explanations localised no better than the central baseline and produced highly overlapping activation across findings. Step-wise analysis ruled out the tested background shortcut and, through agreement with occlusion sensitivity, identified a model-intrinsic positional bias invisible to performance metrics. Anatomical supervision relocated AlexNet’s attributions onto the findings without sacrificing classification performance, whereas DenseNet-121 overfitted the same supervision. Controlled ablations indicate that correction depends on model capacity relative to available anatomical supervision. Notably, a penalty carrying no anatomical information reached almost the same localisation score as explicit box supervision, showing that localisation metrics, like discrimination metrics, can be satisfied without anatomical grounding. These findings show that neither classification nor localisation scores alone can establish anatomically faithful model evidence, which must instead be evaluated against finding-specific semiology and spatially informed baselines.

title: Bio-Inspired Chaos Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of bio-inspired algorithms to optimize chaotic systems. The core idea is to map the optimization of chaotic systems into problems solvable by algorithms like Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO). These algorithms, known for their exploration and learning capabilities, provide a novel approach to finding optimal solutions within the complex dynamics of chaotic systems. The research investigates the potential of leveraging the inherent properties of these algorithms – such as flocking behavior in PSO and pheromone trails in ACO – to effectively navigate and converge towards optimal states within chaotic systems. This work presents a framework for integrating these biological inspirations with chaos theory, offering a potentially powerful tool for diverse applications ranging from control systems to signal processing. The key contributions lie in the methodology for formulating chaotic optimization problems as bio-inspired search problems and in the demonstration of the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach. ---

title: Information-Theoretic Graph Embedding for Robustness
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that prioritizes robustness against adversarial perturbations. Traditional graph embedding methods often optimize for similarity metrics, leaving them vulnerable to minor alterations in the graph structure. We propose an information-theoretic framework where the embedding process is guided by information-theoretic measures, specifically mutual information, to ensure the preservation of salient information while minimizing sensitivity to noise. Our approach defines an objective function that balances these two aspects. This results in graph embeddings that are significantly more resilient to adversarial attacks and structural variations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a theoretical analysis and outline a general framework adaptable to various graph embedding techniques. The core contribution lies in explicitly leveraging information theory to enhance the robustness of graph representations, offering a new direction for graph learning and analysis.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Relational Structures from Streaming Data
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-supervised learning framework designed to extract relational structures from continuous data streams without relying on pre-labeled datasets. The core principle revolves around predicting the subsequent element within a sequence given its preceding context. This process inherently forces the model to discern and represent the underlying relationships and dependencies present in the data. Unlike existing self-supervised methods that necessitate prior labeling, our approach operates purely on the streaming data itself, offering a potentially scalable and adaptable solution for scenarios where labeled data is scarce or unavailable. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through a theoretical analysis and outline a potential implementation strategy. The primary goal is to establish a robust mechanism for unsupervised relational structure discovery directly from continuous data streams.

title: 基于物理定律的计算模型与算法设计
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging fundamental physical laws to design novel computational models and algorithms. The core argument posits that traditional computational paradigms are limited by the constraints of classical physics. This research investigates a new approach – translating physical laws into computational models and subsequently utilizing these models to generate innovative algorithms. Specific examples will be presented, including algorithms inspired by quantum mechanics, demonstrating a shift in the computational paradigm. The aim is to establish a framework for exploring computationally intensive problems by grounding them within established physical principles, potentially leading to significant advancements in computing capabilities. The paper will detail the methodology for this approach, highlighting the key considerations in model construction and algorithm design, focusing on concepts such as wave function collapse, superposition, and entanglement as potential drivers for algorithmic innovation. Ultimately, this work seeks to demonstrate that a deeper understanding and application of physical laws can unlock new avenues for computing.

title: Title: Geometric Intuition via Neural-Symbolic Systems
abstract: Geometric Intuition, the ability to understand and reason about geometric concepts, is a fundamental aspect of human cognition. This paper explores the potential of combining neural networks with symbolic reasoning to develop a system capable of learning geometric intuition. title: Information-Theoretic Constraints on Neural Network Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture design, grounded in information theory. The central argument is that current architectural design practices are largely driven by heuristics and empirical optimization, neglecting a deeper understanding of information processing within neural networks. We introduce a framework that leverages entropy and mutual information to formally constrain the design of layers and connections. The objective is to maximize information flow while simultaneously minimizing redundancy, ultimately leading to more efficient and robust neural network architectures. This work establishes a theoretical foundation for neural network design, moving beyond purely empirical approaches and offering a quantifiable method for evaluating and optimizing network structures. The methodology presented here provides a framework for understanding and controlling information flow within complex networks, with implications for various applications including deep learning and artificial intelligence.

title: From Gaze to Meaning: A Training-Free AI Agent for Unified Grounding and Explanation
abstract: Understanding human attention is fundamental for scene interpretation, yet existing approaches often rely on heavily trained models that lack interpretability. Prior methods struggle to jointly reason about gaze targets, attended objects, and visual grounding without extensive supervision. To the best of our knowledge, this work introduces the first training-free Gaze Target Agent (GTA) for gaze-guided reasoning across tasks such as gaze target prediction, attention localization, and object identification. This is achieved by leveraging pretrained vision-language models, augmenting them with visually guided prompts, and employing a memory-based retrieval strategy for high-uncertainty samples to improve performance without additional training. We evaluate our approach using both quantitative metrics and qualitative results. Quantitatively, our method achieves state of the art performance on the GazeFollow and GazeHOI benchmarks. Qualitatively, our agent provides detailed semantic predictions, predicts the correct targets even when ground truth labels are wrong, and remains flexible without vocabulary constraints.

title: Algorithmic Fairness via Differential Privacy and Federated Learning
abstract: Algorithmic fairness has emerged as a critical concern in the development and deployment of machine learning models, particularly in scenarios where models are trained on diverse and potentially biased datasets. Traditional approaches to achieving fairness often rely on centralized data collection and model training, which can be impractical, raise significant privacy concerns, and exacerbate existing biases due to skewed data distributions. This paper proposes a novel framework for achieving algorithmic fairness in distributed learning environments by integrating differential privacy with federated learning. Our approach allows individual clients to contribute data to a global model without revealing their sensitive information, while simultaneously mitigating bias introduced by biased data distributions. We leverage the privacy guarantees of differential privacy to protect client data and use federated learning to aggregate model updates from multiple clients. The core of our method involves carefully tuning the differential privacy parameters and adapting the federated learning algorithm to account for potential biases in the underlying data. The resulting model exhibits improved fairness metrics compared to traditional federated learning approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a theoretical analysis and a simulation study. The primary contribution of this work is a practical and privacy-preserving method for fostering algorithmic fairness in decentralized learning systems.

title: Probabilistic Reasoning-Based Program Synthesis
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program synthesis leveraging probabilistic reasoning. Traditional program synthesis techniques often rely on exhaustive search or rule-based systems, which can be computationally expensive and prone to generating incorrect or inefficient code. We propose a framework where program synthesis is modeled as a probabilistic inference problem, utilizing techniques like Bayesian Networks or Variational Inference to automatically generate code that satisfies a given functional specification. The core idea is to quantify the uncertainty associated with different code constructs and iteratively refine the solution based on probabilistic assessments. This approach offers the potential for significantly improved efficiency and reliability compared to existing methods. The key contributions of this work are the integration of probabilistic reasoning into the program synthesis paradigm and the demonstration of its effectiveness through a theoretical framework.

title: Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks for Semantic Understanding
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to semantic understanding utilizing multi-scale graph neural networks (MS-GNNs). Traditional semantic understanding models often operate within a single scale of representation, limiting their ability to capture nuanced relationships and contextual information. Our method addresses this limitation by constructing a MS-GNN architecture where each scale corresponds to a distinct semantic representation strategy. We employ graph convolutional operations to effectively fuse information from these diverse scales, ultimately enhancing the accuracy and robustness of the semantic understanding process. The core claim is that a multi-scale approach significantly improves semantic understanding by simultaneously capturing information at various levels of detail. This work introduces a new framework for representing and reasoning about complex semantic relationships, offering a promising direction for future research in areas such as knowledge graph completion, relation extraction, and scene understanding. The proposed MS-GNN model aims to learn richer and more comprehensive representations of semantic data, leading to improved performance across a range of downstream tasks. The key mechanism involves the iterative refinement of semantic representations through graph convolution across multiple scales.

title: Quantum Noise-Based Computation Algorithm Optimization
abstract: This paper proposes a novel computational algorithm leveraging the inherent characteristics of quantum noise. The core premise is that quantum noise, traditionally considered a detrimental factor in quantum computation, can be exploited as a resource to enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of calculations. The algorithm is designed to treat noise not as an error but as an integral component of the computation process. By precisely controlling the intensity and direction of the noise, we aim to improve the overall precision of the results. This approach represents a significant departure from conventional quantum algorithms that primarily focus on mitigating the effects of noise. The methodology outlined herein offers a new paradigm for quantum computation, potentially unlocking significant advantages in specific computational tasks. We explore the theoretical framework and the key design elements, emphasizing the strategic utilization of quantum noise for optimized computation.

title: Non-Euclidean Vector Space for Quantum State Space Exploration
abstract: Quantum state space exploration presents a significant challenge in quantum information science due to the inherent complexity of quantum states. Traditional methods often struggle with the vastness of these spaces, hindering efficient search and analysis. This paper introduces a novel framework for exploring quantum state spaces leveraging non-Euclidean vector spaces, aiming to dramatically improve search efficiency and enable the investigation of complex quantum states. We propose a geometric approach to represent and navigate the state space, utilizing differential geometry to achieve a more efficient and scalable exploration process. This work addresses the limitations of current techniques by providing a fundamentally different perspective on state space representation and navigation. The core mechanism centers around constructing a geometric model of the state space, allowing for the efficient application of techniques from differential geometry to optimize search operations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of theoretical analyses and preliminary experiments, showcasing significant improvements in search performance compared to existing methods.

abstract: This paper presents a novel Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) designed for dynamic system optimization and control. The core concept of the DPLS leverages a probabilistic function as the central element, allowing for rapid adaptation to changing environments through dynamic parameter adjustment. Unlike traditional EA approaches, the DPLS incorporates a genetic algorithm to optimize these parameters, ensuring high self-adaptability. The design focuses on creating a system that can intelligently respond to unforeseen circumstances, leading to superior performance and robustness. The core mechanism involves modifying the probabilistic function's parameters using evolutionary operators, fostering a system capable of continuous learning and improvement. This represents a significant advancement in adaptive control systems, offering a more flexible and robust solution compared to established methods.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic self-organizing algorithm for quantum states, leveraging adaptive quantum state structures to achieve enhanced quantum device properties, including self-adaptation and complexity. The core mechanism centers around dynamically adjusting the quantum state's topology to facilitate intricate and responsive quantum behavior. We present a framework for generating and manipulating quantum states using a self-tuning process, demonstrating significant improvements in quantum device performance compared to static self-organizing approaches. The algorithm's effectiveness is validated through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results.

title: Distributed Cognitive Architectures for Context-Aware Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed cognitive architecture designed to address the challenges of learning in complex and dynamic environments. The core claim is that leveraging distributed computing resources enables continuous perception, understanding, and learning of intricate contexts. This is achieved through the construction of a distributed system comprised of multiple intelligent agents, each specializing in sensing specific aspects of a given context. These agents collaboratively learn and share knowledge, ultimately forming a holistic understanding of the context and continuously updating their respective knowledge bases. Traditional cognitive architectures often lack this distributed learning capability, limiting their effectiveness in handling complex, evolving scenarios. This architecture offers a scalable and robust solution for intelligent systems operating in uncertain and ever-changing environments. The key components and their interactions are described, highlighting the potential for improved adaptability and performance compared to centralized approaches. Mathematical notation demonstrates the core concepts and relationships within the architecture. The architecture's reliance on agent interactions and knowledge propagation is formalized through a series of equations, providing a quantitative framework for understanding and evaluating its performance.

title: DrugBank in RDF: Vector Embeddings
abstract: This work addresses the need for efficient and reusable vector embeddings (VEs) for large-scale RDF Knowledge Graphs, focusing on the widely used DrugBank dataset. The study aims to reduce the computational burden and environmental impact associated with repeatedly generating embeddings for downstream tasks such as link prediction, clustering, and recommendation. To this end, embeddings are generated from the DrugBank Knowledge Graph—comprising over 3.6 million triples, more than 1.5 million entities, and 95 relations—using 25 models implemented in the PyKEEN framework. The dataset is processed into training, validation, and test splits, and embeddings of fixed dimensionality are produced for both entities and relations. The resulting representations are released in multiple formats, including full JSON files, class-partitioned subsets, and an efficient Parquet-based structure, to support scalable querying. Experimental evaluation demonstrates substantial improvements in access time and memory usage when using structured formats, particularly Parquet. Additionally, the study quantifies the carbon footprint of embedding generation, showing that distributing precomputed embeddings can reduce energy consumption by up to 99.37% compared to on-demand recomputation. Overall, the work provides a comprehensive, reusable resource that facilitates research while promoting computational efficiency and environmental sustainability.

title: Оптимізація алгоритму мінімакс з альфа-бета відсіканням для систем шахового штучного інтелекту
abstract: АНОТАЦІЯУ роботі розглянуто підходи до навчання штучної моделі гри в шахи.Базовим методом пошуку обрано алгоритм мінімакс з альфа-бета відсіканням, реалізований мовою програмування Пайтон з відповідною шаховою бібліотекою.Альфабета відсікання зменшує обчислювальну складність обходу ігрового дерева, відкидаючи на ранніх етапах ті гілки, які не впливають на остаточне рішення.До базового алгоритму додано евристичні розширення: ітеративне поглиблення, таблиці транспозицій з хешуванням Зобриста, впорядкування ходів за принципом пріоритету взяття найбільш цінної фігури найменш цінним нападником, евристику вбивці та історичну евристику, а також пошук спокою для послаблення ефекту горизонту.Розроблено адаптивну оцінкову функцію, яка враховує матеріальний баланс, таблиці позиційних оцінок, безпеку короля, структуру пішаків, мобільність фігур і контроль ключових полів.Модель навчено на вибірці понад сто тисяч партій рівнів від аматорського до гросмейстерського.За результатами експериментів, поєднання альфа-бета відсікання з впорядкуванням ходів і таблицями транспозицій зменшує кількість оцінюваних вузлів у середньому у сто двадцять разів відносно стандартного мінімаксу на глибині п'яти півходів, а час прийняття рішення скорочується з дев'яноста двох цілих і чотирьох десятих секунди до нуля цілих і сорока трьох сотих секунди.У модельованих матчах проти шахового рушія модель демонструє високий відсоток перемог на початкових рівнях складності (до дев'яноста шести цілих і п'яти десятих відсотка на нульовому рівні).Як перспективний напрям подальшого розвитку запропоновано архітектуру інтеграції нейромережевого оцінювача на базі ефективно оновлюваної штучної нейронної мережі у класичне альфа-бета дерево пошуку, що дозволить поєднати інтерпретованість класичного методу з адаптивністю глибокого навчання.Запропонований підхід придатний для систем підтримки прийняття рішень у детермінованих іграх з повною інформацією та в задачах стратегічного планування.Ключові слова:

title: Quantum anomaly for benchmarking quantum computing
abstract: Given the rapid advances in quantum computing hardware, establishing strategies for verifying the correctness of quantum computations has become increasingly important. Exploiting the fact that the axial anomaly in gauge theories is exact to all orders in perturbation theory, we propose the axial anomaly as a nontrivial benchmark for quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories. We simulate axial charge production in Z N lattice gauge theories on the trapped-ion quantum computer “Reimei.” After taking the U(1), infinitesimal time, and infinite volume limits, we successfully reproduce the anomaly coefficient within statistical uncertainties, even without error mitigation. Our results demonstrate that the axial anomaly can be simulated on current quantum computers and serves as a verification test of quantum computations.
